title: Godliness, Contentment, and the Good Confession
summary: Paul closes by exposing greed and false teaching, charging Timothy to pursue godliness until Christ appears, to instruct the rich, and to guard the deposit.
historicalContext: The church at Ephesus lived inside a household economy built on slave labor and a civic culture that honored wealthy benefactors with inscriptions and titles. Some within the congregation were slaves, some owned slaves, and some possessed considerable property. Into this setting the false teachers brought speculative controversies and a commercial view of religion, apparently drawing income and patronage from those who followed them. The great city also gave lavish honors to rulers, and the imperial cult hailed the emperor in language that bordered on worship. Paul’s final chapter therefore speaks to concrete pressures: how believing slaves could commend the gospel, how teachers could be tempted by money, how rich members might be tempted to rely on their wealth, and how Timothy could keep faith with a Lord who, unlike every earthly sovereign, alone possesses immortality and reigns without rival.
literaryContext: Chapter 6 completes the household instructions of 5:1–6:2 and then returns to the concern with which the letter opened: teachers who depart from sound words (1:3–7). The material moves in alternating panels. A sharp portrait of the false teachers and their love of gain (vv. 3–10) is answered by a personal charge to Timothy as a “man of God,” rising into a majestic doxology (vv. 11–16). Paul then resumes the subject of wealth from a different angle, addressing those already rich (vv. 17–19), before a brief final appeal to guard the deposit (vv. 20–21). Key words knit the chapter together: gain, godliness, contentment, riches, eternal life, and confession. The chapter thus gathers the letter’s main threads—sound doctrine, godly conduct, and the church’s witness before outsiders—under the light of Christ’s appearing.
themes: Conduct that keeps God’s name from reproach
The ruin wrought by the love of money
The good fight held until Christ’s appearing

outline.title: Servants Who Adorn the Teaching
outline.summary: Believing slaves are to honor their masters so that God’s name is not blasphemed, serving believing masters all the more as beloved brethren.

outline.title: False Teaching and the Love of Money
outline.summary: Paul exposes teachers who reject sound words and treat religion as profit, and sets godly contentment against the deadly desire to be rich.

outline.title: The Charge to the Man of God
outline.summary: Timothy is to flee greed, pursue Christlike virtues, and fight the good fight until the appearing of Christ, whom the immortal King will reveal.

outline.title: Counsel for Those Who Are Rich
outline.summary: The wealthy must reject pride and false security, trust the generous God, and become rich in good works that lay hold of true life.

outline.title: Guard What Has Been Entrusted
outline.summary: Paul’s last appeal urges Timothy to keep the gospel deposit and turn from empty talk falsely called knowledge.

verses.bibleText: Let as many servants as are under the yoke count their own masters worthy of all honour, that the name of God and his doctrine be not blasphemed.

commentary.detailedExplanation:
Paul turns from the elders (5:17–25) to the last group addressed in his household instructions: Christian slaves. The word translated “servants” is douloi, persons legally owned by another. Slaves formed a large part of the population of Ephesus, and many early converts came from their ranks. Paul does not soften their circumstances. “Under the yoke” borrows the language used for oxen harnessed to a plow, a frank acknowledgment that many owners regarded slaves as little more than working animals. Because verse 2 turns separately to believing masters, the present verse chiefly concerns slaves whose owners did not share their faith.

The instruction calls for a deliberate judgment. Such slaves are to “count” their own masters “worthy of all honour.” The honor does not rest on the master’s personal merit, which may have been slight. It is a decision made in faith about how to live within a situation the slave could not alter by his own will. It would show itself in honest work and respectful speech (Titus 2:9–10). Elsewhere Paul encourages a slave to gain freedom if the opportunity comes (1 Corinthians 7:21), so the counsel here is no denial of the desirability of liberty.

The motive is missionary: “that the name of God and his doctrine be not blasphemed.” In Scripture the name stands for God’s revealed character. Unbelieving owners would judge the gospel by the slaves who professed it. If conversion produced insolence or idleness, God would be spoken against because of His people, as Israel once caused His name to be reviled among the nations (Romans 2:24).

This is not a defense of slavery. The same letter lists “menstealers,” those who trade in human beings, among the lawless (1:10). The apostles did not summon powerless believers to a revolt that would have ended in slaughter; they proclaimed a common Creator and a Redeemer who “gave himself a ransom for all” (2:6), truths that hollow out ownership of persons from within. Meanwhile the believing slave who served faithfully under an unjust yoke reflected the Savior who suffered wrong without retaliation (1 Peter 2:21–23).

wordNotes.term: ὑπὸ ζυγόν (hypo zygon) — under the yoke
wordNotes.explanation: The yoke was the wooden beam laid on draught animals, and the image became a figure for oppressive subjection. Paul’s use of it concedes the harshness of the slave’s condition. Scripture uses the same figure for bondage that God breaks, and Jesus offers His own yoke as one that gives rest.

wordNotes.term: τὸ ὄνομα τοῦ θεοῦ … βλασφημῆται (to onoma tou theou … blasphēmētai) — the name of God … be blasphemed
wordNotes.explanation: To blaspheme here is to speak evil of God and His teaching. The concern is reputational in the biblical sense: outsiders form their opinion of God from those who bear His name. The same reasoning governs Paul’s counsel to younger women and his warnings about Israel’s witness.

verses.bibleText: And they that have believing masters, let them not despise them, because they are brethren; but rather do them service, because they are faithful and beloved, partakers of the benefit. These things teach and exhort.

commentary.detailedExplanation:
A second situation brought its own danger. Some slaves belonged to masters who had also come to faith. Such a slave worshiped beside his owner and heard him called a brother. It would be easy to conclude that the ordinary obligations of service no longer applied. The phrase “because they are brethren” states the ground a slave might use for that conclusion, and Paul refuses the inference. Equality in Christ (Galatians 3:28) gives no license to “despise” a believing master by treating him with disrespect.

Instead, such slaves are to “do them service” all the more. The reason Paul offers turns the relationship around: “because they are faithful and beloved, partakers of the benefit.” The masters who receive the benefit of the slave’s labor are believers, loved by God and by the slave himself. The word for “benefit” usually described a patron’s generosity; Paul applies it to a slave’s work. The one with no legal standing becomes a benefactor in Christ’s household.

That reversal shows how the gospel worked on the institution. Paul asked Philemon to receive the runaway Onesimus “not now as a servant, but above a servant, a brother beloved” (Philemon 16), and he told masters to stop threatening, since both master and slave answer to one Lord in heaven (Ephesians 6:9). Where brotherly love governs both sides, the relation of owner and property cannot remain what Roman law said it was. The trajectory of Scripture runs away from slavery and toward the freedom and dignity of every person redeemed by Christ.

“These things teach and exhort” closes the instruction that began at 5:1, much as 4:11 closed an earlier section. Timothy was to explain these duties and urge the believers to live them out.

wordNotes.term: τῆς εὐεργεσίας ἀντιλαμβανόμενοι (tēs euergesias antilambanomenoi) — partakers of the benefit
wordNotes.explanation: Euergesia describes a good deed or kindness, the kind of benefaction for which civic patrons were honored. Here the masters are the ones who receive the benefit, and the benefit is the slave’s service. Paul thus dignifies the slave’s work as an act of kindness to a fellow believer. The noun appears elsewhere only of the healing of the lame man.

wordNotes.term: διδάσκε καὶ παρακάλει (didaske kai parakalei) — teach and exhort
wordNotes.explanation: The pair joins instruction with appeal. Teaching sets out what is true; exhorting presses the hearer to respond in conduct. Timothy’s ministry was to include both, so that doctrine would not remain abstract.

verses.bibleText: If any man teach otherwise, and consent not to wholesome words, even the words of our Lord Jesus Christ, and to the doctrine which is according to godliness;

commentary.detailedExplanation:
For the third time in the letter Paul confronts the false teachers (compare 1:3–11; 4:1–5). “If any man teach otherwise” uses the same rare verb found in 1:3, to teach a different doctrine. The conditional form sounds general, but particular people in Ephesus are in view.

The standard by which that teaching fails is described in two ways. First, it does not “consent” to “wholesome words, even the words of our Lord Jesus Christ.” “Wholesome” means healthy, a medical image that recurs through these letters (1:10; 2 Timothy 1:13; Titus 1:9). Sound teaching nourishes spiritual health; error spreads like a gangrene (2 Timothy 2:17). These words come from Christ Himself. Paul could quote the Lord’s sayings (5:18 echoes Luke 10:7), and he also regarded the apostolic gospel as the message that originates with Christ and is handed on by His messengers. The full title, “our Lord Jesus Christ,” underlines the authority the false teachers were resisting.

Second, the false teacher rejects “the doctrine which is according to godliness.” True teaching accords with and promotes a reverent, obedient life before God. That supplies a practical test. Doctrine is measured by its content first, and its fruit confirms the verdict. Teaching that breeds pride, speculation, and quarrels, as verses 4–5 will show, betrays its own unsoundness.

The verb “consent” originally meant to come toward or attach oneself to something. Error frequently begins as a refusal to draw near to what Christ has said, a preference for one’s own ideas over the plain words of the Lord.

wordNotes.term: ὑγιαίνουσι λόγοις (hygiainousi logois) — wholesome words
wordNotes.explanation: The participle means being healthy or sound. Applied to teaching, it describes words that are true and that produce spiritual health in those who receive them. The image contrasts with the “doting,” literally the sickness, of the false teachers in the next verse.

wordNotes.term: τῇ κατ᾽ εὐσέβειαν διδασκαλίᾳ (tē kat’ eusebeian didaskalia) — the doctrine which is according to godliness
wordNotes.explanation: Eusebeia denotes reverent devotion to God expressed in daily conduct. Teaching “according to godliness” corresponds to such devotion and is designed to produce it. The phrase ties orthodoxy to holy living.

verses.bibleText: He is proud, knowing nothing, but doting about questions and strifes of words, whereof cometh envy, strife, railings, evil surmisings,

commentary.detailedExplanation:
Paul now diagnoses the false teacher. “He is proud” translates a verb that pictures a person wrapped in smoke, so clouded by conceit that he cannot see clearly. The tense describes a settled condition, the same peril Paul warned against in a newly converted overseer (3:6). Despite all his claims to superior knowledge (6:20), such a teacher is “knowing nothing.” He resembles those described at the letter’s opening who wanted to be teachers of the law yet understood neither what they said nor what they affirmed (1:7).

“Doting about questions and strifes of words” carries the medical image forward. The verb means to be sick. Over against the healthy words of verse 3, the false teacher has a morbid craving for controversies and for “strifes of words,” battles fought over terms and fine distinctions. The fables and endless genealogies of 1:4 supplied the material.

The outcome is a list of social poisons: “envy, strife, railings, evil surmisings.” Envy and strife frequently appear together in Paul’s lists (Romans 1:29; Galatians 5:20–21; Philippians 1:15), for rivalry quickly becomes open quarrel. “Railings” translates the word for blasphemies, here abusive speech aimed at other people. “Evil surmisings” are suspicions, the habit of assuming the worst about others’ motives. A congregation absorbed in such disputes soon becomes a place of wary watching.

The atmosphere a teaching creates reveals something about its character. Not every discussion of doctrine is wrong; Paul himself reasoned in synagogues and lecture halls. The question is whether discussion serves truth and the “godly edifying which is in faith” (1:4) or feeds the self. When learning produces arrogance, endless contention, and a suspicious spirit, it has left the path of Christ, whose wisdom is “first pure, then peaceable” (James 3:17).

wordNotes.term: τετύφωται (tetyphōtai) — he is proud
wordNotes.explanation: The verb is related to a word for smoke or vapor and was used figuratively for being puffed up or befogged with conceit. The perfect tense marks a condition that has become fixed. Pride clouds judgment, and the person grows blind to his own ignorance.

wordNotes.term: λογομαχίας (logomachias) — strifes of words
wordNotes.explanation: A compound of “word” and “battle,” describing disputes over terms that generate heat without light. Paul warns elsewhere that such contention profits nothing and subverts hearers.

verses.bibleText: Perverse disputings of men of corrupt minds, and destitute of the truth, supposing that gain is godliness: from such withdraw thyself.

commentary.detailedExplanation:
The list of consequences climaxes in “perverse disputings,” a word suggesting constant friction, people rubbing against one another until everyone is irritated. Paul then traces the trouble to its source in the teachers themselves. They are “men of corrupt minds,” and the participle describes minds that have been ruined and remain so. They are also “destitute of the truth,” literally deprived or robbed of it. These men had once stood among those who heard the gospel; they were inside the church. But by clinging to their own notions they allowed the truth to be taken from them, cooperating in their own loss.

Then comes the motive that exposes them most: they suppose “that gain is godliness.” The Greek order makes the sense clear: they regard godliness as a means of gain. Religion had become a business for them. They may have charged fees for their teaching or drawn support from households they influenced (compare 2 Timothy 3:6; Titus 1:11, “for filthy lucre’s sake”). That is why the letter insists that overseers and deacons must not be lovers of money or greedy of gain (3:3, 8). The poverty of Jesus, who had nowhere to lay His head, refutes every notion that wealth is the badge of God’s favor.

The KJV adds, “from such withdraw thyself.” Many ancient manuscripts lack the clause, yet its counsel agrees with Paul’s instruction elsewhere to turn away from those who have a form of godliness while denying its power (2 Timothy 3:5) and to avoid those who cause divisions for their own appetite (Romans 16:17–18).

Whenever ministry is measured by income, or the gospel becomes a path to personal advantage, the same corruption is at work. Paul’s own example stands in contrast: he coveted no one’s silver, gold, or apparel and worked with his hands to support others (Acts 20:33–35).

wordNotes.term: διεφθαρμένων τὸν νοῦν (diephtharmenōn ton noun) — of corrupt minds
wordNotes.explanation: The perfect participle describes minds that have been thoroughly ruined, with lasting effect. The nous is the faculty of moral and spiritual judgment. When it is corrupted, a person can no longer weigh truth rightly, which explains how these teachers could hold their errors with such confidence.

wordNotes.term: πορισμὸν εἶναι τὴν εὐσέβειαν (porismon einai tēn eusebeian) — that gain is godliness
wordNotes.explanation: Porismos means a means of gain or a source of profit. The false teachers treated religion as a money-making enterprise. Paul will take up their own word in the next verse and give it a new meaning.

verses.bibleText: But godliness with contentment is great gain.

commentary.detailedExplanation:
Paul seizes the false teachers’ own word and turns it against them. They thought godliness was a means of gain; he answers, “godliness with contentment is great gain.” Godliness does bring profit, but of a different order and only when joined to a contented heart. The gain Paul describes has “promise of the life that now is, and of that which is to come” (4:8), and nothing the false teachers collected could compare with it.

The word for “contentment,” autarkeia, was a favorite of moral philosophers in the Greek world. For them it meant self-sufficiency, an inner independence that circumstances could not shake. Paul keeps the idea of freedom from circumstance but changes its source. He had “learned, in whatsoever state I am, therewith to be content,” and he explained the secret immediately: “I can do all things through Christ which strengtheneth me” (Philippians 4:11–13). Christian contentment is sufficiency supplied by God, who makes “all grace abound” so that believers have enough for every good work (2 Corinthians 9:8). It rests on the Lord who has said, “I will never leave thee, nor forsake thee” (Hebrews 13:5).

Such contentment is learned through trust over time. It frees a person from the restless comparison that drives so much of human striving. The contented believer can receive plenty without being owned by it and endure want without bitterness. The Old Testament wisdom writers had already seen the point: “Better is little with the fear of the LORD than great treasure and trouble therewith” (Proverbs 15:16).

A heart at rest in God possesses what money cannot purchase and death cannot remove.

wordNotes.term: αὐτάρκεια (autarkeia) — contentment
wordNotes.explanation: The noun denotes sufficiency, having enough, and by extension the inner state of being satisfied with what one has. In Paul’s usage the sufficiency comes from God rather than from human self-reliance. The related adjective describes the apostle’s own learned contentment.

wordNotes.term: πορισμὸς μέγας (porismos megas) — great gain
wordNotes.explanation: Paul repeats the word for profit from verse 5 and qualifies it with “great.” The repetition is deliberate: true godliness is profitable, but its profit lies in fellowship with God and eternal life, not in income.

verses.bibleText: For we brought nothing into this world, and it is certain we can carry nothing out.

commentary.detailedExplanation:
Paul supports his claim with a truth so plain that it reads like a proverb: “we brought nothing into this world, and it is certain we can carry nothing out.” Job spoke the same words on the day he lost everything: “Naked came I out of my mother’s womb, and naked shall I return thither” (Job 1:21). The Preacher observed it as well (Ecclesiastes 5:15). Birth and death bracket every possession. Whatever a person gathers belongs only to the interval between them.

The argument is simple. If nothing accompanies us in or out, possessions cannot be the substance of life. Jesus warned that “a man’s life consisteth not in the abundance of the things which he possesseth,” and told of a rich fool whose barns were full on the night his life was required of him (Luke 12:15–21). The psalmist added that when the wealthy die, their glory does not descend after them (Psalm 49:17).

This sober realism serves contentment. Holding goods loosely becomes easier when one remembers that they were never permanently ours. What endures is the treasure laid up with God and the character He forms in those who trust Him.

wordNotes.term: οὐδὲν εἰσηνέγκαμεν … οὐδὲ ἐξενεγκεῖν τι δυνάμεθα (ouden eisēnenkamen … oude exenenkein ti dynametha) — we brought nothing … we can carry nothing out
wordNotes.explanation: The two verbs, “bring in” and “carry out,” are built on the same root and frame a human life between entrance and exit. The word “certain” in the KJV is absent from many ancient manuscripts; the sense remains that our inability to take anything beyond death is plain fact.

verses.bibleText: And having food and raiment let us be therewith content.

commentary.detailedExplanation:
From the brevity of life Paul draws a practical standard: “having food and raiment let us be therewith content.” The word for “raiment” means coverings and can include shelter as well as clothing. These are the basic provisions that sustain life. When they are supplied, the believer has what is needed.

Paul does not forbid owning more, and later in the chapter he addresses the rich without asking them to renounce their property (vv. 17–19). He establishes a baseline of need against which desire can be measured. Jacob’s vow asked God for “bread to eat, and raiment to put on” (Genesis 28:20), and Agur prayed to be given neither poverty nor riches but only “food convenient for me” (Proverbs 30:8–9). Jesus taught His disciples not to be anxious about what they would eat or wear, because their Father knows their need and will add these things to those who seek His kingdom first (Matthew 6:31–33).

A life arranged around enough has room for generosity, for rest, and for simplicity in habits that also supports health of body and mind. Contentment here is an act of trust in the Father’s daily care.

wordNotes.term: διατροφὰς καὶ σκεπάσματα (diatrophas kai skepasmata) — food and raiment
wordNotes.explanation: Diatrophē means sustenance or nourishment, and skepasma refers to a covering, which may include both garments and a roof overhead. Together they name the essentials of life. The verb that follows, “we shall be content,” expresses what believers can rightly expect of themselves when these needs are met.

verses.bibleText: But they that will be rich fall into temptation and a snare, and into many foolish and hurtful lusts, which drown men in destruction and perdition.

commentary.detailedExplanation:
Over against contentment Paul sets its opposite: “they that will be rich.” The Greek speaks of those who want, intend, or have resolved to be rich. His target is the settled desire, the determination that wealth must be obtained, rather than the mere possession of means, which he addresses separately in verses 17–19. A person with little money may be ruled by this desire as completely as one with much.

The verse traces a progression of ruin. Such people “fall into temptation,” exposed to constant pressure to compromise honesty and conscience for profit. They fall into “a snare,” the word used elsewhere in the letters for the devil’s trap (3:7; 2 Timothy 2:26). Then they are seized by “many foolish and hurtful lusts,” desires that make no sense in the light of eternity and inflict real damage on the one who indulges them. James describes the same sequence: desire conceives and brings forth sin, and sin brings forth death (James 1:14–15).

The end is described with a violent image. These desires “drown men in destruction and perdition.” The verb was used of boats so overloaded that they began to sink (Luke 5:7). The two nouns that follow both mean ruin. The first can describe the wreck of a life here and now; the second commonly refers to the final perdition of the lost. Together they speak of complete and irreversible loss. Scripture consistently presents the end of the impenitent as destruction, the perishing of life itself, not an endless existence in conscious torment (Matthew 7:13; Romans 6:23). The broad way leads to destruction, and the wages of sin is death.

The path toward that end often begins quietly. Ambition masquerades as prudence, and the pursuit of more crowds out prayer, family, and service. Jesus warned that the deceitfulness of riches chokes the word until it becomes unfruitful (Matthew 13:22).

wordNotes.term: οἱ βουλόμενοι πλουτεῖν (hoi boulomenoi ploutein) — they that will be rich
wordNotes.explanation: The participle describes a purpose or resolve, not a present condition. Paul’s warning falls on those whose aim in life is wealth. The wise man made the same observation: one who hastens to be rich will not go unpunished.

wordNotes.term: βυθίζουσι … εἰς ὄλεθρον καὶ ἀπώλειαν (bythizousi … eis olethron kai apōleian) — drown … in destruction and perdition
wordNotes.explanation: Bythizō means to sink something to the depths. Olethros and apōleia both denote ruin or destruction, and together they intensify the picture of total loss. Apōleia is the regular word for the final perishing of the wicked, set in contrast to everlasting life.

verses.bibleText: For the love of money is the root of all evil: which while some coveted after, they have erred from the faith, and pierced themselves through with many sorrows.

commentary.detailedExplanation:
Paul grounds his warning in a weighty saying: “For the love of money is the root of all evil.” Proverbs condemning avarice circulated widely in the ancient world, yet Paul’s form, with its image of a root, gives the thought its own sharpness. The word “root” stands first in the Greek sentence for emphasis. Roots lie hidden while their branches spread; the visible evils of greed grow from a buried attachment of the heart.

The Greek has no article before “root,” and “all evil” is literally “all the evils.” The sense is that the love of money is a root from which every kind of evil can spring. Paul does not claim that all sin originates in greed alone. Pride, lust, and envy have their own roots. Yet there is no kind of wickedness the love of money cannot produce: lying, theft, fraud, oppression of workers, betrayal of friends, even murder. History and Scripture alike bear witness.

The sin lies in the love, not in money as such. Money can serve God and neighbor, as the instructions to the rich will show (vv. 17–19). The danger arises when money becomes the object of trust and affection. Jesus said that no one can serve God and mammon (Matthew 6:24), and Paul calls covetousness idolatry (Colossians 3:5). The love of money breaks the first commandment by giving the heart to another master and the tenth by craving what is not one’s own (Exodus 20:17).

“Which while some coveted after” uses a verb meaning to stretch out or reach for. Some in Ephesus had reached for money and “erred from the faith,” wandering away from the truth they once confessed. And they “pierced themselves through with many sorrows.” The wounds are self-inflicted. No one forced Balaam to love the wages of unrighteousness, or Achan to hide the silver under his tent (Joshua 7:21), or Gehazi to run after Naaman (2 Kings 5:20–27), or Judas to bargain for thirty pieces of silver. Each found that what he reached for became the instrument of his own grief.

The sorrows Paul has in mind are real and familiar: estranged families, lost health, a troubled conscience, friendships traded for advantage, and above all the loss of faith itself. The remedy is not merely to want less but to love God more, so that money returns to its proper place as a servant.

wordNotes.term: φιλαργυρία (philargyria) — the love of money
wordNotes.explanation: A compound of “love” and “silver,” occurring only here in the New Testament. It names avarice, the heart’s attachment to money. The related adjective describes the Pharisees who derided Jesus and the lovers of self in the last days.

wordNotes.term: ἑαυτοὺς περιέπειραν ὀδύναις πολλαῖς (heautous periepeiran odynais pollais) — pierced themselves through with many sorrows
wordNotes.explanation: The verb means to pierce all around or to impale, and the reflexive pronoun makes the wounding self-inflicted. Odynē denotes pain or anguish. The picture is of one who, grasping at riches, falls upon the very spikes that wound him.

verses.bibleText: But thou, O man of God, flee these things; and follow after righteousness, godliness, faith, love, patience, meekness.

commentary.detailedExplanation:
“But thou” stands emphatically at the head of the sentence. After describing men of corrupt minds and those who will be rich, Paul turns directly to Timothy and sets him in deliberate contrast. He calls him “O man of God,” a title the Old Testament gave to Moses (Deuteronomy 33:1), to Samuel, Elijah, Elisha, and other servants commissioned to speak for the Lord. Timothy is placed in that line. He belongs to God, not to money, and he has been sent on God’s errand. In 2 Timothy 3:17 the same title describes every believer whom Scripture equips for good works, so the charge reaches beyond the pastor to all who are Christ’s.

The instruction has two movements. “Flee these things” points back to the love of money and the vices of verses 3–10: conceit, contention, greed, and the craving to be rich. Some temptations are best met by distance, as Joseph showed in Potiphar’s house.

“Follow after” translates the verb for pursuit, used of a hunter tracking prey or a runner straining toward a goal. Flight alone would leave a vacuum; the heart must be filled with something better. Paul names six qualities in three natural pairs. “Righteousness” and “godliness” describe upright conduct toward others and reverent devotion toward God. “Faith” and “love” stand at the center of Christian life, the trust that receives God’s grace and the love that flows from it. “Patience” and “meekness” join strength with gentleness: patience is steadfast endurance under pressure, and meekness is the mild spirit that can correct opponents without harshness (2 Timothy 2:24–25).

The list reads like a portrait of Christ, and each quality is a fruit of the Spirit rather than an achievement of willpower (Galatians 5:22–23). The same pairing of flight and pursuit recurs in 2 Timothy 2:22, showing how central it was to Paul’s counsel for a young minister.

wordNotes.term: ὦ ἄνθρωπε θεοῦ (ō anthrōpe theou) — O man of God
wordNotes.explanation: The phrase designates one who belongs to God and serves as His representative. In the Old Testament it marks prophets and leaders called to speak for the Lord. Applied to Timothy, it reminds him of his identity and accountability in contrast to those devoted to gain.

wordNotes.term: φεῦγε … δίωκε (pheuge … diōke) — flee … follow after
wordNotes.explanation: Both verbs are present imperatives, calling for continuing action. Pheugō means to run away from danger; diōkō means to pursue earnestly. Paul uses the same verb of his own pressing toward the prize.

verses.bibleText: Fight the good fight of faith, lay hold on eternal life, whereunto thou art also called, and hast professed a good profession before many witnesses.

commentary.detailedExplanation:
Paul now changes the image from flight to contest. “Fight the good fight of faith” uses a verb and noun drawn from the same root, the language of athletic competition and of struggle in battle. The present imperative calls for sustained effort: keep contending. The contest is “of faith,” or literally “the faith,” the struggle that belongs to the Christian life and is waged on behalf of the gospel. Near the end of his own course Paul could write, “I have fought a good fight, I have finished my course, I have kept the faith” (2 Timothy 4:7).

The second command is “lay hold on eternal life.” This verb is in a form that suggests a decisive grasp, as a runner seizes the prize or a drowning man seizes a rope. Eternal life is God’s gift through Jesus Christ (Romans 6:23), never a wage earned by striving. Yet the gift must be received and held. In one sense believers possess it now, for the one who has the Son has life (1 John 5:12). In its fullness it lies ahead, granted at the resurrection when Christ appears (v. 14), when the mortal puts on immortality. Timothy is to grasp now what he will receive completely then.

This life is that “whereunto thou art also called.” God’s calling stands behind the contest; Timothy did not enter it on his own initiative. He also “professed a good profession before many witnesses.” The occasion was probably his baptism, when he publicly confessed Jesus as Lord (Romans 10:9–10), though his commissioning for ministry with the laying on of hands (4:14) may also be in mind. Either way, the confession had been made openly, and many who heard it could hold him to it.

The fight is therefore a matter of living up to a confession already made. Faith is exercised in the daily choices to flee what destroys and pursue what is holy, keeping eyes fixed on Jesus, “the author and finisher of our faith” (Hebrews 12:2).

wordNotes.term: ἀγωνίζου τὸν καλὸν ἀγῶνα (agōnizou ton kalon agōna) — fight the good fight
wordNotes.explanation: Agōn was the word for an athletic contest or any intense struggle, and the verb means to compete or strive. “Good” describes the contest as noble and worthy. Paul applies the image to Christian endurance and to the labor of ministry.

wordNotes.term: ὡμολόγησας τὴν καλὴν ὁμολογίαν (hōmologēsas tēn kalēn homologian) — hast professed a good profession
wordNotes.explanation: Homologia means confession, agreement spoken aloud. The same phrase reappears in verse 13 of Christ before Pilate, linking Timothy’s public confession of faith with his Lord’s. Believers are called to hold fast their confession.

verses.bibleText: I give thee charge in the sight of God, who quickeneth all things, and before Christ Jesus, who before Pontius Pilate witnessed a good confession;

commentary.detailedExplanation:
The tone grows solemn as Paul formally charges Timothy “in the sight of God” and “before Christ Jesus.” He has used similar language in 5:21. Timothy is to understand that his faithfulness is witnessed by the highest court in the universe.

God is described as the One “who quickeneth all things,” the One who gives and preserves life. The description fits the context. Timothy has just been told to lay hold of eternal life, and the God before whom he stands is the source of all life, including the resurrection life He will grant. If confessing Christ were ever to cost Timothy his life, as it would cost Paul his, the God who makes alive would not abandon him. “I kill, and I make alive,” the Lord declared through Moses (Deuteronomy 32:39).

Christ Jesus is described as the One “who before Pontius Pilate witnessed a good confession.” The phrase uses the same words as Timothy’s profession in verse 12, joining the disciple’s witness to his Master’s. When Pilate asked whether He was a king, Jesus affirmed His kingdom and declared that He had come to bear witness to the truth (John 18:36–37). He said little at His trial, and often kept silence (Matthew 27:14), yet what He said was faithful, and He did not retract it under threat of death. Confession in Christ’s pattern is truthful, courageous, and free of self-display.

The mention of Pilate also anchors the gospel in history. The faith Timothy guards concerns real events under a named Roman governor, not timeless myths or speculative genealogies. Christ is “the faithful witness” (Revelation 1:5), and those who confess Him before others will be confessed by Him before His Father (Matthew 10:32).

wordNotes.term: τοῦ ζῳογονοῦντος τὰ πάντα (tou zōogonountos ta panta) — who quickeneth all things
wordNotes.explanation: The verb means to give life or to keep alive. It is used of preserving life from destruction, as when Stephen recalls Pharaoh’s attempt to destroy Israel’s infants so that they might not live. Applied to God, it presents Him as Creator and Sustainer, the One who also raises the dead.

wordNotes.term: ἐπὶ Ποντίου Πιλάτου (epi Pontiou Pilatou) — before Pontius Pilate
wordNotes.explanation: The preposition can mean “before,” in the presence of, or “in the time of.” Both senses are true here, but the parallel with Timothy’s confession before witnesses favors the courtroom sense. Pilate governed Judea from about A.D. 26 to 36.

verses.bibleText: That thou keep this commandment without spot, unrebukeable, until the appearing of our Lord Jesus Christ:

commentary.detailedExplanation:
The content of the charge is “that thou keep this commandment without spot, unrebukeable.” “This commandment” most naturally gathers up the instructions just given: flee, follow after, fight, lay hold. “Keep” means to guard, watch over, and observe faithfully.

The words “without spot, unrebukeable” can be read grammatically with the commandment or with Timothy himself. In practice the two belong together. Timothy is to keep the charge in such a way that neither the charge nor his own life gives anyone grounds for reproach. “Unrebukeable” is the same word used of the overseer in 3:2, “blameless,” one against whom no charge can be made to stick. Peter likewise urges believers to be found “without spot, and blameless” as they look for the day of God (2 Peter 3:14).

The time span is “until the appearing of our Lord Jesus Christ.” The word for appearing, epiphaneia, means a visible manifestation, a public showing forth. In the Greek world it described the sudden appearance of a deity or the ceremonial arrival of a ruler. In the New Testament it refers to the coming of Christ, whether His first advent (2 Timothy 1:10) or His return in glory (2 Thessalonians 2:8; Titus 2:13). By its very meaning the word excludes the idea of a secret or invisible coming. The same Jesus who ascended will come again in like manner (Acts 1:11), and every eye shall see Him (Revelation 1:7). His return will be literal, personal, and visible to all.

That appearing sets the horizon for Timothy’s faithfulness. He is to persevere, not merely through a season of difficulty, but until Christ comes. It also supplies the measure of accountability and the hope that sustains endurance. The church lives between the two epiphanies, guarding the commandment in their light.

wordNotes.term: ἄσπιλον ἀνεπίλημπτον (aspilon anepilēmpton) — without spot, unrebukeable
wordNotes.explanation: Aspilos means spotless, unstained, and is used of the sacrificial lamb and of moral purity. Anepilēmptos means irreproachable, giving no handle for accusation. Together they describe a faithfulness that withstands scrutiny.

wordNotes.term: τῆς ἐπιφανείας (tēs epiphaneias) — the appearing
wordNotes.explanation: Epiphaneia denotes a manifestation that becomes visible. Paul uses it for Christ’s return in glory and once for His incarnation. It describes the public, glorious arrival of the Lord that believers love and await.

verses.bibleText: Which in his times he shall shew, who is the blessed and only Potentate, the King of kings, and Lord of lords;

commentary.detailedExplanation:
Christ’s appearing is something “which in his times he shall shew.” The subject is God the Father, who will display His Son at the appointed moment. “In his times” translates a phrase meaning in its own proper seasons. The timing rests with God, and Scripture gives no warrant for calculating it. Jesus told His disciples that it was not for them to know the times or seasons the Father had kept in His own authority (Acts 1:7). Uncertainty about the hour is no reason for doubt. The event is fixed in God’s purpose; only the date is withheld.

The mention of God’s sovereign timing moves Paul into one of the most exalted doxologies in his letters. God is “the blessed and only Potentate.” “Blessed” here describes God Himself as perfectly happy and complete, the source of all blessedness for His creatures (compare 1:11). “Potentate” means sovereign ruler, and “only” excludes every rival. God is also “the King of kings, and Lord of lords,” literally King over those who reign and Lord over those who rule. Moses called the Lord “God of gods, and Lord of lords” (Deuteronomy 10:17), and Revelation applies the title to the Lamb who conquers (Revelation 17:14; 19:16).

In Ephesus such language would have struck a note against the claims of emperors honored with divine titles. Timothy and the church lived under earthly powers that could threaten and imprison. Paul reminds them that every ruler holds authority only by God’s permission, that He removes kings and sets up kings (Daniel 2:21), and that history moves toward the moment He has chosen to reveal His Son.

wordNotes.term: καιροῖς ἰδίοις (kairois idiois) — in his times
wordNotes.explanation: Kairos denotes an appointed or fitting time; idios means one’s own. God acts at the seasons He has determined. Paul uses the same phrase of the moment God chose to give Christ as a ransom and to manifest His word.

wordNotes.term: ὁ μακάριος καὶ μόνος δυνάστης (ho makarios kai monos dynastēs) — the blessed and only Potentate
wordNotes.explanation: Dynastēs means ruler or sovereign and is used elsewhere of human officials whom God can bring down. Here it is qualified by “only,” presenting God as the one absolute Sovereign. “Blessed” describes His own perfect happiness.

verses.bibleText: Who only hath immortality, dwelling in the light which no man can approach unto; whom no man hath seen, nor can see: to whom be honour and power everlasting. Amen.

commentary.detailedExplanation:
The doxology continues with a description of God’s being that shapes Christian hope at its foundation: He “only hath immortality.” The word means deathlessness, freedom from death. Paul does not say that God shares this quality with all souls or that it belongs naturally to human beings. Immortality belongs to God alone as His own possession; for human beings it is a gift, not an innate property of the soul. God has life in Himself (John 5:26); He is the fountain of life (Psalm 36:9). Every creature’s existence depends moment by moment on Him.

The rest of Scripture speaks consistently on this point. Humanity was formed from the dust and, after the fall, barred from the tree of life lest sinners live forever (Genesis 3:19, 22). Job asks whether “mortal man” can be more just than God (Job 4:17). Believers are to “seek for glory and honour and immortality” (Romans 2:7), which would be pointless if they already possessed it. Christ has “brought life and immortality to light through the gospel” (2 Timothy 1:10). And Paul states when the gift is given: at the last trumpet, when the dead are raised, “this mortal must put on immortality” (1 Corinthians 15:53–54). Until then the dead in Christ sleep, unconscious, awaiting the voice of the Lord who will raise them at His appearing. Christian hope does not rest on a deathless soul but on the living God who raises the dead.

God also dwells “in the light which no man can approach unto.” Light is His garment (Psalm 104:2) and expresses His holiness and glory. At Sinai the people could not draw near, and Moses himself was told, “there shall no man see me, and live” (Exodus 33:20). God is the One “whom no man hath seen, nor can see.” Sinful mortals cannot endure the unveiled glory of His presence.

Yet the gospel bridges this distance without diminishing it. The only begotten Son has declared the Father (John 1:18), and whoever has seen Him has seen the Father (John 14:9). At Christ’s appearing the redeemed, clothed with immortality and made pure in heart, will see God’s face (Matthew 5:8; Revelation 22:4). What no one can now approach, God will open to those He has transformed.

Paul ends where worship always ends: “to whom be honour and power everlasting. Amen.” In a city that offered honors to emperors, Timothy is reminded that honor and eternal dominion belong to this God alone.

wordNotes.term: ὁ μόνος ἔχων ἀθανασίαν (ho monos echōn athanasian) — who only hath immortality
wordNotes.explanation: Athanasia means deathlessness, the state of not being subject to death. The word appears elsewhere in the New Testament only in Paul’s resurrection chapter, where the mortal puts it on at Christ’s coming. God possesses it inherently and alone; human beings receive it as His gift. The parallel title in 1:17 calls God the King “immortal, invisible.”

wordNotes.term: φῶς οἰκῶν ἀπρόσιτον (phōs oikōn aprositon) — dwelling in the light which no man can approach unto
wordNotes.explanation: Aprositos means unapproachable, inaccessible. The image draws on the glory cloud of Sinai and the tabernacle, where God’s presence was too holy for sinful people to enter. God is light, and the redeemed will one day walk in that light without fear.

verses.bibleText: Charge them that are rich in this world, that they be not highminded, nor trust in uncertain riches, but in the living God, who giveth us richly all things to enjoy;

commentary.detailedExplanation:
After the doxology Paul returns to wealth, now addressing those who already possess it. The earlier warning concerned people determined to become rich (v. 9). Here Timothy is told to “charge them that are rich in this world.” The Ephesian church evidently included such members, women able to wear gold and costly clothing (2:9) and householders with property and slaves. Paul does not command them to abandon their wealth, nor does he treat riches as sinful in themselves.

“In this world” means the present age; their riches belong to an order that is passing away.

Two dangers threaten the wealthy. The first is to be “highminded,” arrogant, inclined to look down on others and to assume that money confers superior worth or wisdom. The second is to “trust in uncertain riches.” Wealth gives an impression of security that it cannot sustain. The proverb says riches “make themselves wings” and fly away like an eagle (Proverbs 23:5). Death finally separates every owner from his goods.

The proper object of trust is God, “who giveth us richly all things to enjoy.” The words “the living” are absent from many ancient manuscripts, but the point stands. The same God the rich are tempted to forget is the One who supplied their abundance. He gives “richly,” matching and surpassing their wealth with His generosity, and He gives “to enjoy.” This clause also answers the ascetic teachers who forbade God’s good gifts (4:3–4). The safeguard against misusing them is not refusal but gratitude to the Giver, so that confidence rests in Him rather than in the gifts. As Jeremiah said, the rich man is not to glory in his riches but in knowing the Lord (Jeremiah 9:23–24).

wordNotes.term: ἐπὶ πλούτου ἀδηλότητι (epi ploutou adēlotēti) — in uncertain riches
wordNotes.explanation: Literally “on the uncertainty of riches.” Adēlotēs means indefiniteness or unclearness, that which cannot be counted on. Paul’s phrasing shifts the focus from riches as solid possessions to their unreliability as a foundation. The psalmist warns against setting the heart on increasing wealth.

wordNotes.term: πάντα πλουσίως εἰς ἀπόλαυσιν (panta plousiōs eis apolausin) — richly all things to enjoy
wordNotes.explanation: Plousiōs, “richly,” echoes the word for the rich, setting God’s generosity alongside human wealth. Apolausis means enjoyment or benefit. God’s gifts are given for His creatures’ delight, a truth that guards against both greed and joyless asceticism.

verses.bibleText: That they do good, that they be rich in good works, ready to distribute, willing to communicate;

commentary.detailedExplanation:
Having warned the rich against pride and false trust, Paul tells them what to do. Four expressions follow, and together they reinterpret wealth as an instrument for good. They are to “do good,” using their means actively for others. They are to “be rich in good works,” a play on words that redirects the ambition for riches toward a different kind of abundance. They are to be “ready to distribute,” generous and open-handed. And they are to be “willing to communicate,” ready to share and to enter into fellowship with those in need.

In the cities of Asia the wealthy commonly gave public gifts, built monuments, and funded festivals, and in return they received inscriptions and honorary titles. Paul’s instruction redirects that culture of benefaction. The believer’s generosity seeks the good of the needy, not public acclaim (Matthew 6:2–4). It reflects the God “who giveth us richly” (v. 17), so that those who have received much become channels of His kindness.

The last word suggests more than writing checks. It implies a willingness to share life with others, to stand beside the poor in the fellowship of the church instead of remaining aloof. The early believers in Jerusalem had all things in common and distributed as each had need (Acts 2:44–45). Paul reminded the Ephesian elders of the Lord’s saying, “It is more blessed to give than to receive” (Acts 20:35).

wordNotes.term: εὐμεταδότους, κοινωνικούς (eumetadotous, koinōnikous) — ready to distribute, willing to communicate
wordNotes.explanation: Eumetadotos describes one who gives readily and liberally. Koinōnikos, related to koinōnia, describes a person disposed to share and to enter into fellowship. Both words occur only here in the New Testament. Paul elsewhere urges giving with simplicity and reminds believers not to forget to share.

verses.bibleText: Laying up in store for themselves a good foundation against the time to come, that they may lay hold on eternal life.

commentary.detailedExplanation:
Generosity has a future. By doing good the rich are “laying up in store for themselves a good foundation against the time to come.” The verb means to store up treasure, and Paul joins it to the image of a foundation. The metaphors mix, but the meaning is clear. Treasure given away in love does not vanish; it becomes a sure footing for the future. Jesus taught the same truth: lay up treasures in heaven, where moth and rust do not corrupt and thieves do not break in, for where the treasure is, the heart will be also (Matthew 6:19–21). He told a rich young ruler to sell what he had and give to the poor so that he would have treasure in heaven (Luke 18:22).

“The time to come” looks ahead to the day of reckoning when Christ appears (v. 14) and gives to every one according to his works (Matthew 16:27). Good works do not purchase salvation. They are the fruit of grace and the evidence of where a person’s heart has been set. Uncertain riches offer no ground to stand on at that day, but a life spent in faithful stewardship rests on God’s promise.

The goal is “that they may lay hold on eternal life.” In place of “eternal life,” many ancient manuscripts have “the life which is life indeed.” Either way the phrase recalls verse 12. Life propped up by possessions is a poor imitation of real life. The life Christ gives, begun now and completed at the resurrection, is the only life that deserves the name.

wordNotes.term: ἀποθησαυρίζοντας … θεμέλιον καλόν (apothēsaurizontas … themelion kalon) — laying up in store … a good foundation
wordNotes.explanation: The participle means to store away as treasure. Themelios is a foundation, the base on which a building stands. Paul merges the images to describe a treasure that functions as solid ground for the future. Jesus’ parable of the wise builder uses the same idea of a sure foundation.

wordNotes.term: τῆς ὄντως ζωῆς (tēs ontōs zōēs) — eternal life (literally “the life that is truly life”)
wordNotes.explanation: Ontōs means really or truly. The reading favored by many ancient manuscripts contrasts real life with the counterfeit security of wealth. The same adverb describes the true widow earlier in the letter.

verses.bibleText: O Timothy, keep that which is committed to thy trust, avoiding profane and vain babblings, and oppositions of science falsely so called:

commentary.detailedExplanation:
The letter closes with an urgent, personal appeal: “O Timothy.” Only here in the letter does Paul address him by name in this way, and the effect is like a hand laid on his shoulder. Everything Paul has written is gathered into a single command: “keep that which is committed to thy trust.” The underlying noun, parathēkē, was a legal and commercial term for property deposited with someone for safekeeping, to be returned intact when required.

The deposit is the gospel, the sound doctrine received from Christ through the apostles. Paul uses the same image twice in his second letter to Timothy (2 Timothy 1:12–14), and there he adds that the guarding is done “by the Holy Ghost which dwelleth in us.” Guarding does not mean hoarding. Timothy is to pass the deposit to faithful men who will teach others also (2 Timothy 2:2). What must not happen is alteration.

Guarding the deposit requires turning away from two things. The first is “profane and vain babblings,” godless and empty chatter, talk that sounds spiritual but has no substance and no holiness (4:7; 2 Timothy 2:16). The second is “oppositions of science falsely so called.” In the English of 1611, “science” meant knowledge in general, from the Latin word for knowing. Paul is not speaking about the study of the natural world. He refers to the antitheses, the contrary claims and arguments, of what was falsely named knowledge. The false teachers boasted of a superior insight hidden from ordinary believers. Their teaching involved speculative myths and genealogies (1:4), ascetic prohibitions (4:3), and perhaps, as later in Ephesus, a spiritualized denial of the future resurrection (2 Timothy 2:18).

Against every counterfeit, the church holds to the faith “once delivered unto the saints” (Jude 3). True knowledge is to know God and Jesus Christ whom He has sent (John 17:3), and it always humbles the knower rather than inflating him.

wordNotes.term: τὴν παραθήκην φύλαξον (tēn parathēkēn phylaxon) — keep that which is committed to thy trust
wordNotes.explanation: Parathēkē means a deposit entrusted to another’s care, and phylassō means to guard or protect. The image presents the gospel as a treasure belonging to God, held in trust by His servants and answerable to Him. Paul is confident that God likewise guards what Paul has committed to Him.

wordNotes.term: ἀντιθέσεις τῆς ψευδωνύμου γνώσεως (antitheseis tēs pseudōnymou gnōseōs) — oppositions of science falsely so called
wordNotes.explanation: Antithesis means a contrary assertion or opposing argument. Pseudōnymos means falsely named, and gnōsis means knowledge. The phrase describes teaching that claimed the name of knowledge but did not deserve it. Paul warns elsewhere that knowledge without love puffs up.

verses.bibleText: Which some professing have erred concerning the faith. Grace be with thee. Amen.

commentary.detailedExplanation:
The final sentence explains why the warning matters: “Which some professing have erred concerning the faith.” The verb “professing” means making a claim or public announcement, the same word used in 2:10 of women “professing godliness.” These people advertised their superior knowledge, and in doing so they “erred,” literally missed the mark. Paul used the same verb at the letter’s opening of those who had swerved from love and a good conscience (1:6). The letter ends where it began, with the danger posed by teachers who depart from the truth (1:3–7, 19–20). Claims to advanced knowledge led some away from the faith entirely, a sober reminder that intellectual pride can carry a person far from Christ.

Then comes the shortest of benedictions: “Grace be with thee.” The best ancient manuscripts read “with you,” plural. Although the letter is addressed to Timothy, Paul expected it to be heard by the congregation, and the blessing reaches them all. Many manuscripts also lack the closing “Amen.”

Grace is the fitting last word. Timothy’s fight, the church’s witness, the generosity of the rich, and the faithfulness of slaves all depend on the unmerited favor of God in Christ. Paul closes his other letters to Timothy and Titus the same way (2 Timothy 4:22; Titus 3:15).

wordNotes.term: ἠστόχησαν (ēstochēsan) — have erred
wordNotes.explanation: Astocheō means to miss the target or to deviate from a goal. It occurs only in the Pastoral Letters, always of people who strayed from sound teaching. The image is of an archer whose arrow flies wide.

wordNotes.term: ἡ χάρις μεθ᾽ ὑμῶν (hē charis meth’ hymōn) — grace be with thee
wordNotes.explanation: Charis is God’s undeserved favor and enabling help. The plural pronoun, found in the earliest manuscripts, extends the blessing to the whole church that would hear the letter. The same short form closes Colossians.

teachingNotes.openingQuestion: If someone examined only how you handle money and possessions, what would they conclude you believe about God?
teachingNotes.mainPoint: Sound doctrine produces godliness, and godliness joined with contentment frees believers from greed to pursue righteousness, give generously, and hold fast their confession until Christ appears.
discussionQuestions: Why does Paul connect false teaching so closely with the desire for gain?
How does Christian contentment differ from mere resignation or a lack of ambition?
What does it mean to flee some things and pursue others, and why are both needed?
How does the truth that God alone has immortality shape Christian hope about death and resurrection?
What would it look like for wealthy believers in your setting to be rich in good works?
commonMisunderstandings: Paul does not call money itself evil; he condemns the love of money and the settled resolve to be rich.
The counsel to slaves does not endorse slavery; the gospel’s brotherhood and the condemnation of slave trading in 1:10 work against the institution.
“Who only hath immortality” does not teach that human souls are naturally deathless; immortality is God’s alone and is given to the redeemed at the resurrection.
The “science falsely so called” refers to counterfeit spiritual knowledge, not to the study of the natural world.
teachingNotes.emphasis: Hold together truth and life: doctrine that is sound produces godliness, contentment, generosity, and steadfast confession, all lived in view of Christ’s visible appearing.
teachingNotes.closingAppeal: Flee the restless love of money, take hold of the life that is truly life, and keep your confession unstained until the King of kings reveals His Son.

evangelisticNotes.mainDoctrinalTheme: God alone possesses immortality, and through Jesus Christ, who witnessed a good confession and will appear again, He offers eternal life as a gift to those who lay hold of it by faith.
flow: We brought nothing into the world and can carry nothing out; possessions cannot secure life.
The love of money promises fulfillment but ends in sorrow and destruction.
God alone has immortality; human beings are mortal and depend on Him for life.
Through Christ, God offers eternal life, received in full at His appearing and the resurrection.
Lay hold of that life now by confessing Christ and following Him.
simpleIllustrations: A traveler packing for a one-way journey learns that nothing in the house can come along; only what has been sent ahead will be waiting.
A deposit placed in trusted hands is returned intact; the gospel entrusted to the church must be passed on unaltered.
evangelisticNotes.appealQuestion: Will you stop seeking security in what you must leave behind and lay hold of the eternal life God offers in Jesus Christ?
cautions: Do not present contentment as indifference to poverty or injustice.
Do not imply that generosity purchases salvation; good works express faith and lay up treasure by grace.
Do not suggest that the soul is naturally immortal or that the dead are already receiving their reward.

reflectionQuestions: Where am I tempted to measure godliness, success, or God’s favor by material gain?
What would it take for me to say honestly that food and covering are enough?
Which desire do I need to flee, and which virtue should I pursue in its place this week?
How does my daily work commend or discredit the name of God before those who do not believe?
What part of the gospel entrusted to me am I most tempted to dilute, and how can I guard it?
